rows.question: Why is R1 18k and not something round like 10k?
rows.text:
The resistors and capacitors work as a team: they set where the filter starts reducing higher-frequency signals. [R1] is 18 kΩ because, with [R2], [C1] and [C2], it puts that point near the 1 kHz target; the measured cutoff is 996 Hz, and the filter’s sharpness also passes [block:b2].

For these values: 1/(2π√(18kΩ·30kΩ·10nF·4.7nF)) ≈ 1.00 kHz. If [R1] were 10 kΩ and the others stayed the same: 1/(2π√(10kΩ·30kΩ·10nF·4.7nF)) ≈ 1.34 kHz. So 10 kΩ is rounder, but it would move the filter’s cutoff away from the target.

rows.question: Why is C2 smaller than C1?
rows.text:
C2 is smaller to set the filter’s shape, not because it is a different kind of capacitor. In this Sallen-Key circuit, C1 and C2 work with R1 and R2 together: their values set the cutoff frequency and Q, which describes how sharp the filter’s knee is [block:b2].

For these resistor values, the capacitor ratio helps give the target Q of 0.707:
Q = √(R1·R2·C1·C2) / [C2·(R1+R2)]
= √(18kΩ·30kΩ·10nF·4.7nF) / [4.7nF·(18kΩ+30kΩ)] ≈ 0.706 [R1] [R2] [C1] [C2].

So C2 is 4.7nF while C1 is 10nF to meet that Q target; the simulated cutoff is also on target at 996Hz [block:b2]. Equal capacitors could work too, but the resistor values would need to be chosen differently.

rows.question: How did they get 3.3 nF for this capacitor?
rows.text:
The capacitor was chosen to make [R1] and [C1] set the filter’s cutoff near the [block:b2] target of 2 kHz. Rearranging the cutoff formula gives:

C = 1/(2π·24 kΩ·2 kHz) ≈ 3.32 nF

They used the nearby value 3.3 nF for [C1]. With that value, the cutoff is about 1/(2π·24 kΩ·3.3 nF) ≈ 2.01 kHz, close to the simulated 2.02 kHz.

rows.question: Why is R2 ten times R1?
rows.text:
[R1] feeds the signal into the amplifier, and [R2] helps set how strongly it comes out. The op-amp keeps their shared connection close to ground, so the signal current through [R1] also flows through [R2]. Making [R2] ten times larger gives about ten times the output, with the signal flipped over—this is the job of the inverting amplifier [block:b2].

100 kΩ ÷ 10 kΩ = 10. The simulation shows the result: a 100 mV input becomes a 1 V output, and the gain target of 10 passes.

rows.question: What is the 1.1k emitter resistor for, and why that value?
rows.text:
[R4] is the emitter resistor: it makes changes in transistor current raise the emitter voltage, which opposes further current change. This local negative feedback stabilizes the bias and reduces gain sensitivity to transistor variation. At the simulated current, it drops about 1.06 V: 0.966 mA × 1.1 kΩ ≈ 1.06 V [net:B2_N_E].

Its value also sets the gain together with [R3]. Using the block’s estimate, |gain| ≈ 5.6 kΩ / (1.1 kΩ + 26 mV / 0.959 mA) ≈ 4.97, close to the measured 4.92 [block:b2]. So 1.1 kΩ gives roughly the target gain of 5 while providing emitter feedback.

rows.question: What does the 10 nF on the control pin do? Nothing seems to depend on it.
rows.text:
[C2] is a bypass capacitor: it helps keep the 555’s control reference steady by shunting electrical noise to ground. That reference sets the switching thresholds; in this oscillator it is normally two-thirds of the supply, or ⅔ × 9 V = 6 V.

The simulated control net stays at 6 V during the transient [net:B1_N_CTRL], so the capacitor has no visible effect on the clean, ideal waveform. It can matter if noise on the supply or control reference would otherwise cause unwanted switching. The oscillation timing is mainly set by [C1], [R1], and [R2] [block:b1].

rows.question: What is the op-amp doing here? It has no gain resistors.

Moving [C1] to ground would make a different filter network and change its cutoff and Q. rows.question: How does the 555 keep oscillating?
rows.text:
The 555 acts like a switch controlled by the voltage on [C1]. While [C1] charges through [R1] and [R2], [U1] holds its discharge path off. When the capacitor reaches two-thirds of the 9 V supply, [U1] switches the output low and lets [C1] discharge through [R2]. At one-third of the supply, it switches the output high and charging starts again. That repeating cycle makes [net:B1_OUT] oscillate, as described by [block:b1].

The switching levels are 9 V ÷ 3 = 3 V and 2 × 9 V ÷ 3 = 6 V; the capacitor’s simulated range on [net:B1_N_THR] is 3.01–5.99 V. The estimated rate is 1.44 ÷ ((7.5 kΩ + 2 × 15 kΩ) × 39 nF) ≈ 985 Hz, close to the simulated 990 Hz.

rows.question: Why did I need the op-amp after my RC filter?
rows.text:
[R1] and [C1] form a low-pass filter: they reduce higher-frequency parts of the signal at [net:N2]. [U1] is wired as a voltage follower, so its output [net:N3] tracks that filtered voltage without adding voltage gain.

The follower’s high input impedance means it draws very little current from the filter; its lower output impedance helps drive a following circuit without that circuit changing the filter’s response. The filter’s cutoff is about 723 Hz: 1/(2π·10 kΩ·22 nF) ≈ 723 Hz.

Whether you strictly needed the op-amp depends on what is connected after [net:N3]; that load isn’t shown here. If nothing follows, or the next input barely loads the filter, the RC filter could work on its own.

rows.question: Why put a follower after a divider?
rows.text: The divider sets the voltage, but a load connected directly to it can draw current and shift that voltage. The follower buffers it: its high input impedance draws very little from the divider, while its lower output impedance can drive the load. Here, [net:B1_OUT] feeds [U1] in [block:b2], and the output is fed back to the inverting input; both nets simulate at 2.5 V. The simulation has no varying input signal or shown load, so it doesn’t demonstrate the buffer’s performance under load.

rows.question: Can I get a gain of 10 by changing the emitter resistor?

It will change, so rerun AC at 1 kHz to check. The collector is currently at 6.63 V [net:B2_N_C]; increased current will pull it lower.

Likely for this specific buffer, but not guaranteed to perform identically. [block:b2] is a unity-gain follower: [net:B1_OUT] carries a 1 V, 1 kHz sine, and [net:B2_OUT] follows it at 1 V. With ±12 V supplies [net:VCC] and [net:VEE], the signal is well within the rails.

The required slew rate is 2π·1 kHz·1 V ≈ 0.0063 V/µs, a modest demand; an LM358 is generally suitable for a unity-gain buffer at this signal level. Compared with [U1], its higher input bias current can matter with a high-impedance source, and its lower speed can matter at higher frequencies. This slice has no LM358 model or real-source impedance, so simulating with an LM358 model is needed to verify an exact comparison.

rows.question: What happens if I connect a 100 ohm speaker to the output?
rows.text:
Assuming the speaker’s other terminal connects to [net:GND], [C2] blocks DC but lets the signal reach it. The 100Ω load and 10µF [C2] make a high-pass filter: fc = 1/(2π·100Ω·10µF) ≈ 159Hz. At 1kHz, an ideal estimate gives 0.995·100/√(100² + (1/(2π·1kHz·10µF))²) ≈ 0.983V at [net:B2_OUT].

That voltage would mean about 0.983V/100Ω ≈ 9.8mA of signal current. That is roughly 9.8mA/1.95mA ≈ 5 times [Q1]’s no-signal emitter current, so the output may distort or clip; [block:b2] is a buffer, but this is a much heavier load than the current simulation tests. The exact loaded waveform needs a transient simulation with the speaker connected.

rows.question: If I set the source to 5 kHz, how big will the output be?
rows.text:
Changing [V1] to 5 kHz leaves its amplitude at 1 V. Using the measured cutoff and Q of [block:b2], an ideal second-order low-pass predicts an output of about 39.6 mV amplitude:

r = 5,000/996 ≈ 5.020; |H| = 1/√[(1−r²)²+(r/0.706)²] ≈ 0.0396; 1 V × 0.0396 ≈ 39.6 mV.

That’s an estimate: the slice doesn’t include a simulated value for the output. Run an AC analysis covering 5 kHz and probe [net:B2_OUT] for the actual result.

rows.question: If I connect a 1k load to N1, does it still give the same voltage?
rows.text:
No. [R1] and [R2] make a voltage divider, and [net:N1] is currently 2.88 V. If the 1 kΩ load connects from [net:N1] to ground, it gives the voltage another path to ground and pulls it much lower.

The load is in parallel with [R2]: 4.7 kΩ × 1 kΩ ÷ (4.7 kΩ + 1 kΩ) ≈ 0.825 kΩ. Then the divider gives about 9 V × 0.825 kΩ ÷ (10 kΩ + 0.825 kΩ) ≈ 0.69 V.

rows.question: Why is the output 90 degrees behind the input?
rows.text:
The lag is the normal response of this second-order low-pass, not an inversion by the op-amp: [U1] is wired as a non-inverting buffer, while the RC network sets the filter’s phase. At the filter’s cutoff, its two poles combine to give about −90° of phase shift; [B2] is at 996Hz cutoff, and the simulation is at 1kHz, so it is essentially at that point.

For a second-order low-pass, at cutoff the normalized response is \(H(j\omega_c)=1/(j/Q)=-jQ\), which has phase −90°. That matches the simulated input at 0° on [net:B1_OUT] and output at −90.1° on [net:B2_OUT]. The output magnitude is also 705mV for a 1V input, consistent with being near the cutoff knee.

rows.question: The output is 1 V but it looks upside down compared to the input. Is that right?
rows.text:
Yes—“upside down” is exactly what an inverting amplifier does: when the input swings up, the output swings down. The output is also 10 times larger here, as expected for [block:b2].

[net:B1_OUT] has a 100 mV input, and [net:B2_OUT] has a 1 V output with the opposite direction. The gain magnitude comes from [R2] ÷ [R1] = 100 kΩ ÷ 10 kΩ = 10, so 100 mV × 10 = 1 V.

rows.question: Why is the gain a bit less than 1?
rows.text:
An emitter follower tracks the base, but its base-emitter junction needs a small change in voltage to change the transistor current. So when the emitter rises, the base-emitter voltage shrinks a little, and the emitter rises slightly less than the input.

Here the input is 1 V and the output is 995 mV at 1 kHz, so gain = 995 mV / 1 V = 0.995 [net:B1_OUT] [net:B2_OUT]. The emitter resistor [R3] helps set how strongly the transistor responds; the simulated gain is just under 1 [block:b2].

rows.question: Why does it switch at 3.49 V going up but 2.49 V going down?
rows.text:
[U1] is used as an inverting comparator: it compares the input [net:B1_OUT] with the threshold at [net:B2_N_P]. [R1] and [R2] set the threshold, while [R3] feeds the output back to it. That feedback creates the two switching points in [block:b2].

The threshold is \((9/16 + V_{\text{out}}/33)/(1/16 + 1/7.5 + 1/33)\), using the resistor values in kΩ. The denominator is \(0.2261\ \text{kΩ}^{-1}\). With the output high at 7.52 V, the threshold is \((9/16 + 7.52/33)/0.2261 \approx 3.50\text{ V}\), matching the measured 3.49 V. With the output low at 0.0174 V, it is \((9/16 + 0.0174/33)/0.2261 \approx 2.49\text{ V}\) [net:B2_OUT].

So as the input rises past the upper threshold, the output goes low and pulls the threshold down; as it falls past the lower threshold, the output goes high and lifts the threshold again.

rows.question: How do I fix my filter?
rows.text:

rows.question: Why is the gain 11 here?
rows.text:
It isn’t 11 in this circuit: [block:b2] is an inverting amplifier, so its signed gain is −R2/R1. The “+1” belongs to the gain formula for a non-inverting amplifier, which is wired differently.

Here, [R2] feeds the output back to the inverting input and [R1] brings the signal to that input; the other input is grounded. So −100 kΩ/10 kΩ = −10. The minus sign means the output is inverted: [net:B1_OUT] is 100 mV and [net:B2_OUT] is 1 V, giving a magnitude gain of 1 V/100 mV = 10, with 180° phase shift. The block’s measured gain is 10.0, which passes its target.

rows.question: Why is R1 connected to ground?
rows.text:
[R1] connects the feedback path to ground, making it part of a voltage divider with [R2]. That divider feeds a fraction of the output back to the amplifier; the amplifier adjusts its output so that fraction matches the input [block:b2].

Here, 100kΩ ÷ 10kΩ = 10, and 1 + 10 = 11, so the gain is 11. That means the simulated 100mV input becomes a 1.1V output. [R1] sets how much of the output is fed back.

rows.question: Why would I use a Schmitt trigger instead of the plain comparator?
rows.text:
A plain comparator has one switching threshold, so noise near that point can make its output flip back and forth (“chatter”). A Schmitt trigger adds hysteresis: feedback through [R3] shifts the threshold depending on the output’s current state. That makes it useful for turning a slow or noisy signal into cleaner transitions.

Here, [block:b2] switches at about 3.49 V in one direction and 2.49 V in the other, a 1.00 V gap (3.49 V − 2.49 V = 1.00 V). After it switches, the input must cross the other threshold before it switches back.

rows.question: If I raise the input to 1 V, will the amplifier clip?
rows.text:
Assuming 1 V means peak input at [net:B2_OUT], [block:b3]’s gain is \(1+[R4]/[R3]=1+100\,\text{kΩ}/10\,\text{kΩ}=11\), so a clean output would need to reach \(1\,\text{V}\times11=11\,\text{V}\) peak at [net:B3_OUT]. That is only \(12\,\text{V}-11\,\text{V}=1\,\text{V}\) below each supply rail [net:VCC] [net:VEE]. Since the TL072’s output swing is limited before it reaches the rails, clipping is plausible, but this slice doesn’t show its limit at that signal level.

Run a transient analysis with a 1 V peak input and check whether the tops of [net:B3_OUT] flatten. If you meant 1 V RMS, the ideal output would be \(1\,\text{V}\times\sqrt{2}\times11\approx15.6\,\text{V}\) peak, which exceeds the ±12 V supplies.

rows.question: And what would happen if I made them the same?
rows.text:
If [C1] and [C2] were equal, [R1] and [R2] would make Q about 0.484, below [block:b2]’s 0.707 target. That means the response would be less maximally flat around its knee.

Q = √(R1·R2)/(R1+R2) = √(18kΩ·30kΩ)/(18kΩ+30kΩ) ≈ 0.484.

The cutoff also depends on which value you use for both capacitors: if both were 10nF, fc ≈ 1/(2π·√(18kΩ·30kΩ·10nF·10nF)) ≈ 685Hz; if both were 4.7nF, fc ≈ 1/(2π·√(18kΩ·30kΩ·4.7nF·4.7nF)) ≈ 1.46kHz.
